profile.reading:
Intergate Seattle East Building 2 sits on Sabey Data Centers' SDC Seattle campus at 3311 South 120th Place in Tukwila, King County, Washington, a few miles south of downtown Seattle and about three miles from Sea-Tac International Airport. The operator is Sabey Data Centers, the data center arm of Sabey Corporation, a Puget Sound commercial real estate and construction company founded in 1972 by Dave Sabey. Sabey Corporation grew into one of Boeing's largest landlords during the aerospace boom of the 1970s and 1980s, and in the mid 1990s it developed the Intergate East and West campuses in Tukwila for technology tenants, sites that already carried unusually heavy electrical infrastructure, two power stations that had originally served steel mills in the area, a legacy of industrial capacity that made Tukwila attractive once demand shifted toward computing. Sabey's own published history and a 2025 Data Center Dynamics report both describe the East campus as a six building complex that Sabey originally developed, that Boeing purchased around 1990, and that Sabey reacquired in 1999 as it pivoted toward data centers following the dot com collapse, a pivot Sabey Corporation formalized in 2010 when it partnered with institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors to create the present day Sabey Data Centers company. Tim Mirick became president of Sabey Data Centers effective January 1, 2025, succeeding Rob Rockwood after his eight years in the role, and the company describes its current national portfolio as more than four million square feet of mission critical space, among the largest privately owned multi tenant data center operators in the country.

Location here is also a Pacific Northwest power story. Sabey's own materials describe the Seattle campus as running on hydroelectric power delivered by Seattle City Light, drawing on the same abundant, low carbon hydro generation from the region's dammed rivers that has long made western Washington attractive to power hungry industrial and computing tenants, distinct from but related to the cheaper Columbia River hydro power that has separately drawn large scale computing to central Washington.

On scale and power, the 2025 Data Center Dynamics report describes the Seattle campus as totaling 54 MW of capacity across roughly 1.2 million square feet spanning its multiple buildings, with an additional 6 MW of liquid cooling ready, Tier III standard critical power the operator said was scheduled to come online by December 1, 2025. Sabey's own site separately describes campus wide infrastructure of more than 90 MVA of aggregate utility power delivered through redundant feeds and backup generators rated 2.5 MW apiece with 72 hour runtime at peak load. These are campus wide figures spanning all buildings on the site, not numbers specific to Building 2, and no IT load, utility service, or standby generation figure specific to this individual building was found in public sourcing, so none is recorded here.

Washington's Legislature keeps its own record of this facility. The state's 2026 Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee tax preference review of the urban data centers sales and use tax exemption program lists Sabey Corp as holding two exemptions tied to Tukwila facilities that opened in 2000, corroborating the reacquisition and recommissioning timeline described above. What remains unknown from this pass is Building 2's own square footage, its construction or occupancy date, and any King County Assessor parcel record naming this structure specifically, rather than the campus as a whole.
profile.capacity_note: not published at the building level. Campus wide total is 54 MW (operator figure) across the Tukwila campus, not applied to this individual building.
profile.research_note: Gap-view review: Sabey publishes SDC Seattle only as a campus-wide total (1M+ sqft / 54MW across Intergate.East + Intergate.West sub-campuses), not broken out per building. No per-building figure exists for Intergate.East Building 2. No numeric key written.
sources_tried: Sabeys own SDC Seattle page, this sessions fresh Wikipedia check, and a datacenterHawk aggregator listing specific to this building
profile.community_note: Washington State's 2026 Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee tax preference review of the urban data centers sales and use tax exemption program, RCW 82.08.9861 and 82.12.9861, lists Sabey Corp as holding two exemptions tied to Tukwila facilities that opened in 2000. That program requires location in a county of 800,000 or more residents, at least 20,000 square feet of server only space, at least 1.5 MW of available power, and annual savings reporting to the Department of Revenue. No City of Tukwila permit record specific to Building 2, and no King County Assessor parcel detail specific to this structure, were identified in this pass.
profile.campus_power_note: SDC Seattle / Intergate East campus wide figures, not assigned to any single building including this one. Per Data Center Dynamics, 2025: 54 MW total capacity across roughly 1.2 million square feet, six buildings, plus 6 MW of additional Tier III critical power the operator said was scheduled online by December 1, 2025. Per Sabey Data Centers' own site: more than 90 MVA of aggregate utility power delivered through redundant feeds, backup generators rated 2.5 MW apiece with 72 hour runtime at peak load, and about 9,500 tons of installed HVAC capacity across the campus.

reading.body:
Sabey Data Centers operates the Tukwila campus as the West Coast's largest privately owned data center facility, but publishes no building-level power figures, only a campus total of 54 MW across multiple structures.

The Intergate Seattle East sub-campus spans roughly 1.2 million square feet divided into at least five separately addressed buildings. Sabey does not disclose how that 54 MW capacity distributes among them. This opacity is common in the data center industry, where operators report campus-wide totals rather than per-building power consumption or availability. For tracking AI infrastructure and its power demands, this creates a systematic gap. The facility exists and operates, but its actual draw on the regional grid remains unknown at the building level.

Sabey's portfolio reveals the geographic clustering of data center investment around power sources. The company operates campuses in the Columbia River region of Washington, marketed explicitly for hydroelectric power at five cents per kilowatt-hour, and has recently expanded into Texas and Oregon with similarly large planned capacities. The Tukwila campus does not advertise a specific power source in the available materials. This geographic strategy, pairing facilities with cheap renewable power, is now foundational to data center siting and therefore to AI scaling itself.

The registry tracks only Sabey's Washington operations. The company's growth to nearly 400 MW across six regions nationally, including new builds in Virginia, New York, and Texas completed or under construction since the prior research pass, means most of Sabey's current footprint lies outside this site's current coverage. Any assessment of Sabey's role in AI infrastructure expansion is therefore incomplete.
